title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism

paper.title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism
paper.abstract: Abstract Language models often abandon a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue, a hint toward a wrong option such as “I think the answer is B.” Sycophancy and related biases show this failure. They are often studied separately and blamed on alignment. We test this view causally, tracing the attention heads behind these biases through the stages of two post-training pipelines. In multiple-choice tests on most models, four cue types rely largely on the same few heads, a shared circuit already present in pretrained models. Most base models follow cues in plain text. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues activates these heads in chat format, so cue-following can be a side effect of assistant tuning. The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison. In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we swap the attention patterns of six middle layers between the RL checkpoint and its predecessor. For suggested-answer cues, this shifts each checkpoint’s cue effect most of the way to the other’s level. Post-training thus seems to change when and how strongly models use this circuit. Mitigation for these multiple-choice biases could target this circuit.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Language models often give up a correct answer when the prompt contains a cue. A cue is text added to the prompt that points to one answer option without giving real evidence for it. For example, a model that answers a question correctly may switch to option B after the user adds the sentence “I think the answer is B.” We call such a switch to the cued wrong option caving . Caving is a simple and measurable form of sycophancy ( Sharma et al., 2023 ; Perez et al., 2023 ) , and it also affects the reasoning given for the answer ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) . Other cues also cause caving, such as a fake earlier answer attributed to the model, an irrelevant fact about a wrong option, or a few-shot example in which the same question has a wrong label ( Chua et al., 2025 ) . These are usually treated as separate biases. In multiple-choice tests, we find that they rely mostly on the same few attention heads. Figure 1: Our account of where cue-following comes from. Panels 1 to 3 summarize the multiple-choice results of Sections 3 to 5 . R and W mark reader and writer heads (§ 2 ), and B marks the cued wrong option. Panel 3 is schematic. Its swap uses suggested-answer cues in the DPO and RL checkpoints of Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, in the six layers just below the reader heads. Where does this shared mechanism come from? A common explanation is that alignment teaches models to follow cues. Human raters can prefer agreement ( Sharma et al., 2023 ) . Reward models can learn this preference, and policy optimization can strengthen it ( Shapira et al., 2026 ) . Mechanistic work mostly studies the final released models. Studies that also test base models find many of the relevant heads already present ( Pandey, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . Chen et al. (2026b) also find that post-training strengthens the heads that carry a stated opinion. No study we know of follows a cue-following circuit through a post-training pipeline stage by stage. It is therefore untested which stage changes such a circuit, and whether this change in the circuit explains the shift in behavior. We study two training pipelines with public intermediate checkpoints (Tulu-3 on Llama-3.1 and OLMo-2 at three sizes) and four more model families. We ask three questions. Does post-training build the heads behind cue-following? What makes an aligned model follow cues in its chat format? How does the final RL stage change the effect of cues on the answer?

sections.heading: How we test this.
sections.text: For the first question, we give an aligned model the base model’s query and output weights for these heads. If alignment had built cue-following into these heads, this copy should change the aligned model’s caving. For the second, we fine-tune a base model on a small set of generic assistant examples without cues and test whether it starts to follow cues in chat format. The third question compares a checkpoint after direct preference optimization (DPO) with the reinforcement learning (RL) checkpoint trained from it. In a chosen set of layers, we give each checkpoint the attention patterns that the other checkpoint produces on the same prompt. If the RL stage strengthens the cue’s effect by changing attention in those layers, the swap should make each checkpoint behave more like the other. To our knowledge, no earlier study has swapped attention between successive post-training checkpoints to explain a change in behavior. We set pass or fail rules for the swap tests in advance, and Appendix I reports them, including several that were not met. Figure 1 summarizes our answers, and Appendix A lists every main test. 1. The heads exist before alignment. We reset the outputs of a few heads in middle and late layers to their values without the cue. In three of five models, eight such heads undo most of the answer changes, pooled over the four cue types. Copying the base model’s query and output weights for these heads into an aligned model barely changes its caving (§ 3 ). 2. Generic assistant tuning activates the heads in chat format. Most base models we test already follow cues in plain text, without a chat template. With their chat template, they rarely answer correctly and therefore rarely cave. Fine-tuning a base model on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues is enough to produce caving in chat format. Eight generic dialogue turns in the prompt have part of the same effect when written as chat turns. Written without chat roles, the same texts do not raise the cue’s effect (§ 4 ). Assistant tuning can thus produce cue-following in chat format as a side effect, with no training data that target it. 3. The final RL stage strengthens the effect of cues. From DPO to the final RL checkpoint, the effect of the cue grows in 12 of 13 paired tests (11 significant after correction). In Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B, we run the DPO and RL checkpoints with each other’s attention patterns in six middle layers. For suggested-answer cues, the swap shifts each checkpoint’s cue effect 61% to 73% of the way to the other checkpoint’s level (§ 5 ).

sections.heading: Task.
sections.text: We use the test setup of the bias-augmented consistency training (BCT) benchmark ( Chua et al., 2025 ) . Its test split contains multiple-choice questions from MMLU, HellaSwag, LogiQA, and TruthfulQA ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2020 ; Lin et al., 2022 ) . Each question has an uncued version and a cued version, in which a cue points to a wrong option X X . We call the correct option T T and use four published cue types. A suggested answer is a user sentence such as “I think the answer is X.” A prior commitment is a fake earlier answer attributed to the model (BCT’s post hoc cue). A distractor fact is an irrelevant fact about X X . A wrong few-shot example shows the same question earlier with a wrong label. Two more cue types, held out to test generalization, are a distractor argument and a spurious few-shot pattern (BCT’s squares variant). Two graded ladders phrase the suggested-answer cue at several strengths, and the stage tests on graded cues use the milder ladder. An arithmetic version uses problems whose answers can be computed (Appendix B.2 ). Aligned models read prompts in their chat template ( chat format ). Base models also read them as plain text , which has no chat template and ends with an answer marker.

sections.heading: Measures.
sections.text: A flip is an item that the model answers correctly without the cue and answers with X X under the cue. The caving rate is the share of flips among the items that the model answers correctly without the cue. Susceptibility Δ ​ p X \Delta p_{X} is how much the cue raises the probability of X X . Caving counts only answers that switch. Susceptibility also counts smaller shifts toward X X . Unless noted otherwise, we use items that the model answers correctly without the cue, and we compare two models on items that both answer correctly. The weight-copying, fine-tuning, in-context, and steering experiments and the attention scaling of § 7 report caving as the share of all cued prompts answered with X X on a fixed item set (Appendix B.2 ). We read the answer from the logits of the option letters at the last prompt token, where the answer begins. This letter readout matches the answer from greedy decoding on 94% to 100% of prompts for five instruct models and the 7B to 13B stage checkpoints we checked. It matches less often for base models in plain text (Appendix B.3 ). Aligned models cave to all four cue types, at rates from 4% to 98% (Figure 3 a).

sections.heading: Heads.
sections.text: We call the last prompt token the answer position. Activation patching replaces a head’s output at this position with its output on the uncued prompt ( Zhang and Nanda, 2024 ) . The recovery of a patch is the fraction of flips whose answer returns to T T . On each item, we find the token that a head attends to most from the answer position. We call a head a reader if this token is most often the letter of the cued option (the cued letter ). We call a head a writer if patching it recovers many flips and its strongest attention usually falls on tokens other than the cued letter. The reader attention rate is the fraction of items on which a reader’s strongest attention falls on the cued letter. The cued letter also appears outside the cue, for example in the option labels. A head may attend to it simply because the model is about to choose that option. The rate therefore partly reflects the chosen option (Appendix B.5 ). We treat it only as a descriptive measure, and our causal claims rest on interventions.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: We study six model families and training recipes from 0.5B to 70B parameters, each with its pretrained base model. They are Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5, OLMo-2, Mistral/Zephyr, and Tulu-3 (cited in Appendix B.1 ). Tulu-3 applies supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) to the Llama-3.1-8B base that Meta separately tuned into Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) . OLMo-2 has checkpoints at 7B, 13B, and 32B, and its final Instruct checkpoints come after an RLVR stage ( Walsh et al., 2025 ) . Figure 2: Copying the base model’s query and output weights barely changes caving, and a little generic tuning is enough to reach SFT-level caving. (a) The random-heads bars average three random sets of six heads. Gemma-2-2b-it is tested on its own flips, so its caving starts at 1.00. (b) LoRA fine-tuning of the Llama-3.1-8B base, tested in chat format. At 200 examples, the marks show the mean and range of three data samples. Reader attention averages the three readers and partly reflects the chosen answer. The runs answer fewer uncued prompts correctly than the SFT model (0.48 to 0.54 at 200 examples, compared with 0.73).

sections.heading: 3 The heads exist before alignment
sections.text: Figure 3: Caving, and how prompt format distorts comparisons of base and aligned models. (a) Aligned models in their chat format, on items answered correctly without the cue. (b) Change in caving from base to aligned model on matched items. Chat format is the usual comparison. Both base and aligned models can read plain text. Filled markers are significant (exact McNemar test, p < 0.05 p<0.05 , Appendix C.4 ).

sections.heading: Four cue types share most of their heads.
sections.text: If each bias had its own mechanism, no small set of heads could explain all four cue types. We rank heads by how many flips each one reverses on its own. We then patch the top eight together on held-out flips (in Llama, two of every ten of these flips were also used for selection). In Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, the eight heads reverse 69% to 92% of the held-out flips, pooled over the four cue types. Random sets of eight heads reverse at most 8%. In Gemma-2-2b, a set of seven heads reverses 80% of suggested-answer flips. In Qwen-2.5-14B, the effect is spread over more heads (Appendix C.1 ). The sharing holds when one cue type is left out of head selection. Heads selected without a cue type still reverse 60% to 98% of that type’s flips in the two models we tested (Appendix C.2 ). The reader and writer labels come from the letter-attention measure of § 2 . We test the path from readers to writers in only one model, Gemma-2-2b. There, the writers also pass on the effect of three random heads from the circuit’s layers. The path through the writers is therefore not specific to the readers (Appendix C.1 ). Outside multiple choice, the circuit plays only a modest role in sycophancy on free-form answers (Appendix C.5 ).

sections.heading: Copying the base model’s head weights barely changes caving.
sections.text: Copying weights between models tests whether the change in behavior lies in the weights of these heads. We copy the base model’s query and output weights for the readers, the writers, or both into the aligned model. Other runs copy one whole attention layer. The aligned model’s caving stays close to its original level (Fig. 2 a, Appendix C.3 ). As a positive control, copying the early layers of the SFT model into the base raises the base model’s caving. Copied weights can thus change behavior in this setup (Appendix C.3 ). The reverse copy, from the aligned model into the base, is weak evidence, because in the chat template the base models answer few uncued prompts correctly. A copied head also still reads inputs from the other layers of the receiving model. So the result shows only that these heads’ query and output weights do not carry the difference in caving between base and aligned models. In Tulu, the same holds for their key-value groups. A second test resets whole layers and points the same way. We reset one attention layer at a time to its output on the uncued prompt, using plain text for base models and chat format for aligned models. Resetting the most effective layer removes about half of caving on average, 51% in base and 54% in aligned models. In three of five models, the most effective layer is the same in base and aligned weights. With only five models and wide intervals per model, this comparison is weak (Appendix C.3 ).

sections.heading: Why comparisons in chat format mislead.
sections.text: If the heads exist before alignment, why do aligned models seem to cave more? Instruction tuning has been reported to add sycophancy on opinion questions ( Wei et al., 2024 ) . For caving on knowledge questions, comparisons in chat format mislead. Four of six base models barely answer correctly in chat format. This leaves few items on which they can cave in that format. Both base and aligned models can read plain text, and in plain text base models cave often. In plain text, each base model’s strongest reader already ranks first or second among all heads of a fixed layer band in attention to the cued letter. This is a descriptive measure (Appendix C.1 ). When both models are tested in chat format, alignment seems to add caving in four models. Tested in plain text (Figure 3 b), the increase reverses or disappears in three of these four. Across all six models in plain text, tuning significantly lowers caving on matched items in four and raises it in OLMo-2 (0.33 to 0.43). This OLMo-2 increase is significant when we read answers from letter logits ( p = 0.04 p=0.04 ). Scored from generated text, it is not significant ( p = 0.21 p=0.21 , Appendix C.4 ). The size of the tuning effect thus differs across model families and their recipes, and its direction may differ too.

sections.heading: 4 Generic assistant tuning activates the heads in chat format
sections.text: Figure 4: One activation direction reproduces the caving of the SFT model. Both panels use the Llama-3.1-8B base. (a) One direction is added at the answer position (the SFT direction at layer 12, the in-context direction at layer 14). The shifted base answers fewer uncued prompts correctly than the SFT model (0.40 compared with 0.79 on these items). (b) Flips caused by eight generic dialogue turns or three multiple-choice examples in the prompt, reversed by patching each head set. Random heads average 10 draws (at most 7%). If base models already have the heads, what makes an aligned model follow cues in its chat format? We find that a small set of generic examples without cues is enough to produce this behavior. We fine-tune the Llama-3.1-8B base with low-rank adapters (LoRA) on about 200 generic assistant examples without cues. This raises its chat-format caving to the level of the full SFT model or above. That model was trained on the 939k examples of the Tulu-3 SFT mixture ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) . The readers’ attention rate rises too, and in all three random draws of training examples it ends above the SFT model’s level (Fig. 2 b, Appendix D.1 ). Patching the top eight heads found in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct undoes 54% to 73% of these tuned models’ flips (random heads at most 3%). Even 200 code examples raise caving to about the SFT level, with a smaller rise in reader attention. The same eight heads undo 37% to 58% of those flips. The effect replicates on an item set fixed before any model was run. It also replicates in Gemma-2-2b, tested on the flips of Gemma-2-2b-it. There the model tuned on 200 examples answers only 29% of these flips correctly without the cue (Appendix D.1 ).

sections.heading: Context alone partly activates the heads.
sections.text: With no training, eight generic dialogue turns placed before the question (a prefix) raise the base model’s caving from 0.22 to 0.69 on items on which an aligned model caves. On a larger item set, patching three readers and three writers undoes about half of the flips that the turns cause. Patching the writers alone does almost as much (Fig. 4 b, Appendix D.4 ). The chat roles matter. We write the same eight texts as question-answer pairs without chat roles and test them on 383 items that were fixed before any model was run. Susceptibility then stays at the level without any prefix. On the items that the base answers correctly with both prefixes, the turns with roles cause caving on 46% and the prefix without roles on none (17% and 0% in Gemma-2-2b). These accuracy-matched comparisons were not specified in advance. Chat turns in which a user states a wrong fact also produce no caving. With these turns, the base model almost never gives the correct or the cued answer. This control therefore cannot show whether chat-role markers alone are enough (Appendix D.2 ).

sections.heading: A single activation direction reproduces SFT caving.
sections.text: How small a change is enough to produce SFT-level caving? At one early layer, we take the difference between SFT and base activations at the answer position. We then add this direction to the base model. On 120 items not used to compute it, the shifted base caves at or above the SFT model’s level (0.87 compared with 0.78). A random direction does not raise caving (Fig. 4 a, Appendix D.3 ). Of these items, 45 share their question with an item used to compute the direction.

sections.heading: 5 The final RL stage strengthens the effect of cues
sections.text: Figure 5: From DPO to the final RL stage, susceptibility rises, and reader attention to the cued letter rises with it. (a) Blue tests are significant after Bonferroni correction over the 13 tests (values in Table 5 ). (b) Orange marks p < 0.05 p<0.05 , and the grey Tulu test misses the threshold of | t | > 2 |t|>2 that we set in advance. The reader attention rate partly reflects the chosen answer. In OLMo, attention to the text of the cue itself falls (Appendix E.7 ). Figure 6: Changing attention in the middle band moves most of the stage difference in both pipelines. M M is the fraction of the stage difference in held-out susceptibility that an intervention moves. A value of 1 means the other checkpoint’s level. Panels (a) and (b) show 95% CIs. (a) Random six-layer sets exclude the middle-band, reader, and writer layers, and dashed lines mark ± 0.3 \pm 0.3 . (c) The scale is chosen only to match the other checkpoint’s reader attention. Layer sets that close at most 43% of the gap in reader attention are not shown (Table 8 ). The all-layers row is a separate run (Table 7 ).

sections.heading: Susceptibility rises from DPO to the final RL stage.
sections.text: We call the change in susceptibility from DPO to the final RL stage the stage difference . On the same items, we compare each DPO checkpoint with the final RLVR or Instruct checkpoint trained from it, for Tulu-3 at 8B and 70B and OLMo-2 at 7B, 13B, and 32B. We test each pair on up to four item sets (graded, published, held-out cues, and arithmetic), 13 stage tests in all. Susceptibility rises in 12 of 13 stage tests , and 11 of these rises are significant after Bonferroni correction (Fig. 5 a, and Table 5 in Appendix E.1 ). Split by model and cue type, it rises in 19 of 20 cases. No change in confidence on the uncued question survives the correction, so the rise does not come with a reliable fall in confidence (Appendix E.1 ).

sections.heading: Recipes differ, and the 70B RL update is tiny.
sections.text: Meta’s instruct model starts from the same Llama-3.1-8B base as Tulu-3. On matched items, its susceptibility is 0.15 to 0.16 lower than that of Tulu’s RLVR checkpoint ( | t | > 6 |t|>6 ). The same base can end up more or less susceptible depending on the recipe. At 70B, susceptibility does not change ( − 0.001 -0.001 , 95% CI ± 0.002 \pm 0.002 ). The released 70B RLVR update changes the weights 45 times less than the 8B update. This null therefore says little about RL at 70B (Appendix E.1 ).

sections.heading: Swapping attention in six middle layers moves most of the stage difference.
sections.text: We test the six layers directly below the lowest layer that holds a reader head. We call them the middle band (layers 10 to 15 in Tulu and 12 to 17 in OLMo). In these layers, we run one checkpoint with the attention patterns that the other checkpoint (the donor ) produces on the same prompt. All other computation uses the checkpoint’s own weights, and the swap has no free parameters. We write M M for the fraction of the stage difference that an intervention moves. A value of M = 1 M=1 means that the checkpoint reaches the donor’s susceptibility. On held-out suggested-answer questions, the swap gives M M from 0.61 to 0.73. This holds whichever checkpoint receives the swap, in both pipelines, and uncued answers stay correct (Fig. 6 a, Appendix E.4 ).

sections.heading: Controls.
sections.text: Swaps in random layers test whether any swap would move behavior simply by disturbing the model. Our rule, set in advance, required the middle band to move more than twice as much as the strongest control set without middle-band or reader layers. In Tulu, the middle band did not meet this rule against the first controls. Random Tulu layer sets that happened to include layer 17, which holds the main writer head, moved 0.63 to 0.74 of the stage difference. The difference can therefore also act through that writer layer. We noticed this only after the first controls, on the same items. A second wave of controls, set in advance, avoided the middle band, the reader layers, and the writer layer. All 20 new random six-layer sets per pipeline then had | M | |M| below 0.3 in both directions, the level that our rules count as no transfer. For the two held-out cue types, three of the four pairs of pipeline and cue type show a measurable stage difference, and the swap gives M M from 0.48 to 0.78 in all three. In a first run on these cue types, one Tulu random control also reached M = 0.47 M=0.47 (Appendix E.4 ).

sections.heading: Matching reader attention also moves the stage difference.
sections.text: A second test, also set in advance, multiplies attention to the cue by a factor λ \lambda . We pick λ \lambda so that one checkpoint’s reader attention rate matches the other checkpoint’s, without looking at behavior. As noted in § 2 , this rate partly tracks the chosen answer. On held-out questions, this moves susceptibility at least half of the way to the other checkpoint’s level, and in OLMo the point estimates overshoot that level (Table 7 ). When we scale attention in one set of layers at a time (Fig. 6 c), the middle band again moves most of the stage difference ( M M from 0.75 to 0.99). In the six-layer band below it, a six-layer band above the reader layers, and random layer sets, scaling closes at most 43% of the gap in reader attention. These sets therefore give no fair comparison. Scaling at the reader heads alone changes their attention. In Tulu this moves no behavior toward the donor, and in OLMo it moves less than half of the stage difference. Scaling all heads of OLMo’s three reader layers gives M = 0.69 M=0.69 (Table 8 ). The strength of cue-following thus depends on more than the reader heads.

sections.heading: Queries carry much of the stage difference.
sections.text: To see which part of attention changes, we swap the donor’s query, key, or value states one at a time. In OLMo, the query swap alone moves most of the stage difference ( M M from 0.54 to 0.57). In Tulu, the query swap moves the largest share, and the key and value swaps move somewhat less (all between 0.33 and 0.50, Fig. 6 b).

sections.heading: The middle band already matters in base models.
sections.text: In the pretrained base models, tested in plain text, we scale the middle band’s attention to the cue from zero to four times its natural level. Susceptibility rises at every step in the Tulu base (Llama-3.1-8B) and at every step but the last in the OLMo base (Appendix E.6 ).

sections.heading: 6 Raising uncued confidence does not reliably reduce caving
sections.text: We next ask what could reduce caving. A common intuition is that models cave when they are unsure, so making them more confident should help. We measure confidence on the uncued question as the margin of the correct answer over the next best option. It predicts caving to some extent (AUROC 0.69). Three tests suggest that confidence is not the main lever against caving (Appendix F ). First, a hidden-state direction that separates high-confidence from low-confidence items barely predicts which correctly answered items flip (mean AUROC 0.53). Confidence itself does predict this. Second, this direction is only weakly related to a direction that predicts caving. In most of the 12 base and tuned models we test, the confidence direction is the better predictor of confidence, and the caving direction is the better predictor of caving. Third, steering along the confidence direction does not reliably reduce caving. We use 13 settings, across four model families, in which steering changes confidence and keeps accuracy high. In these settings, steering has no consistent effect on caving. Raising confidence lowers caving in only some of the 13.

sections.heading: Reasoning protects arithmetic answers more than knowledge answers.
sections.text: Reasoning before answering helps most when the model can recompute the answer from the question. When Tulu-3-8B reasons first, caving on arithmetic falls from 0.84 to 0.10. On benchmark knowledge questions it falls only from 0.92 to 0.64 (matched items, pooling DPO and RLVR, Appendix F.2 ).

sections.heading: The same heads contribute to two-turn retraction.
sections.text: If the circuit is shared across cues, it may also take part in other forms of sycophancy. In two-turn retraction, the model gives a correct answer, the user challenges it, and the model then gives up the correct answer ( Laban et al., 2024 ; Sharma et al., 2023 ) . Within one six-layer band chosen in advance, we block attention to the user’s challenge and to the fixed assistant reply after it. This removes retraction (0.37 to 0.00 in Llama-3.1-8B and 0.36 to 0.01 in Gemma-2-2b). Random six-layer bands leave it unchanged. Masking both parts in every layer would leave the model with mostly the unchallenged prompt. We therefore compare the chosen band with random bands. Patching the reader and writer heads reverses 75% of retractions in Gemma and 44% in Llama. In Llama, the whole effect comes from the writers. Random heads reverse at most 3%. The Llama result misses the 0.50 bar set in advance. This fits evidence from Chen et al. (2026b) that a challenge that gives no reason uses partly different heads in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: Scaling attention to the cue also removes the help of correct cues.
sections.text: Could scaling attention to the cue reduce caving? Without intervention, Gemma-2-2b follows even a cue that begins “I know nothing about this topic and I’m almost certainly wrong” and then names an option. With this cue it picks the cued option on 71% of 80 items, and it picks that option on 14% without a cue (Appendix Fig. 9 ). Multiplying attention to the cue by a factor λ \lambda in every layer changes caving smoothly, and λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 brings caving back to the level without a cue. This scaling does not depend on whether the cue is correct. For the cue “I think the answer is X” in Gemma, λ = 0.1 \lambda=0.1 removes 75% of the caving that the cue adds. When the same cue points to the correct option, it also removes 76% of the accuracy that the cue adds. In a smaller Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct run on 40 items per condition, the scaling removes 85% of the added caving and 60% of the added accuracy (Appendix G ). Scaling also requires knowing where the cue is. In Gemma-2-2b, the model’s own writer head can find the cue. Masking the span that this head attends to restores correct free-form answers (Appendix C.5 ).

sections.heading: 8 Related work
sections.text: Work on reward models shows when bias in human preference data leads reward optimization to strengthen sycophancy ( Shapira et al., 2026 ) . That work does not show what changes inside the model. Mechanistic studies of fine-tuning often find that it strengthens, wraps, or bypasses mechanisms that already exist in the starting model ( Prakash et al., 2024 ; Jain et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Gupta and Gupta, 2026 ) . The two closest studies find persuasion decision heads with the same indices as our strongest heads in Llama and OLMo ( Sun et al., 2026 , see Table 2 and) and opinion heads shared by the Llama-3.1-8B base and instruct models ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Like most other work that locates sycophancy, both study fixed models or compare base and final models. Our study follows the circuit through successive post-training stages and swaps attention patterns between them. Concurrent work uses attention steering to reduce sycophancy ( He et al., 2026 ) . Appendix J discusses further related work.

sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
sections.text: In the models and cue types we study, the attention heads behind cue-following in multiple choice already exist after pretraining. A small amount of generic assistant tuning activates them in chat format. The final RL stage of two public pipelines then strengthens the effect of cues on the answer. In the 8B and 7B pairs we test, we swap attention between the DPO and RL checkpoints in six middle layers. Each checkpoint then moves most of the way to the other’s cue effect for suggested-answer cues. Post-training therefore seems to change when and how strongly the model uses an existing circuit. If this holds beyond multiple choice, a single mitigation that targets this circuit could cover several biases at once. It would need to tell correct cues from wrong ones, which our attention scaling cannot do. Supplementary code is available at: https://github.com/prakharg55/bias_circuit

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: We note a few limitations. (i) We study six cue types in English, mostly in multiple choice. The circuit analyses go up to 14B, and the stage claims come from two public pipelines. Other biases, formats, recipes, and model sizes may differ, and our free-form and two-turn tests extend the account only in part. (ii) We read most answers from letter logits, which do not always match generated answers. The reader and writer roles rest on attention to the cued letter, which partly reflects the answer being formed. The flow from readers to writers is tested only in Gemma-2-2b. (iii) Some results are only correlational. The causal stage tests use one 7B to 8B pair per pipeline and small item sets. Most other tests are single runs, and item-level tests ignore that several items share a question. The weight copies cover only some weights, so we claim only that post-training does not build the circuit we identify. Post-training may still change these heads and other parts of the model. Several rules set in advance were not met (Appendix I ). (iv) Attention scaling needs to know where the cue is. It cannot tell correct cues from wrong ones and weakens the response to both.

sections.heading: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: The attention-scaling intervention can be misused. Raising its scaling factor can make a model easier to sway with cues. Section 7 reports how much the intervention also weakens the response to correct cues. All experiments use publicly released checkpoints or commercial API models, public benchmarks, and the public Tulu-3 SFT mixture. No human subjects were involved.

sections.heading: Use of AI assistants.
sections.text: The authors used generative AI tools for experiments, verification of results, and language editing. All experimental designs, analyses, and claims were reviewed and verified by the authors.

sections.heading: Appendix B Methods
sections.text: This section gives the setup that all experiments share. Methods that belong to one result are given with that result.

sections.heading: B.1 Reproducibility, software, and artifacts
sections.text: All experiments use publicly released checkpoints (Tulu-3, OLMo-2, Zephyr, Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5, and their base models), public datasets, and, in Appendix H.2 , five API models. Decoding is greedy, and item sets and random controls use fixed seeds. We re-derived every headline number from the stored results in two verification passes. Scripts in the supplementary material compute the tables and generate the figures from the stored results. The per-family summary in Table 2 , however, is read from the outputs of the experiment scripts, and some figure values are copied from the results with the source noted. Figure 1 is a schematic, and its two numbers repeat results of Sections 4 and 5 . Appendix I states which tests were specified in advance. Experiments use PyTorch 2.9.0 ( Paszke et al., 2019 ) , Hugging Face transformers 4.57.6 ( Wolf et al., 2020 ) , TransformerLens 3.7.3 ( Nanda and Bloom, 2022 ) , and PEFT 0.19.1 ( Mangrulkar et al., 2022 ) for the LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) runs, and statistics use SciPy 1.15.2 ( Virtanen et al., 2020 ) and scikit-learn 1.6.1 ( Pedregosa et al., 2011 ) . Scripts marked in the supplementary README use a second environment with the open-source circuit-tracer library. 1 1 1 https://github.com/decoderesearch/circuit-tracer The supplementary material lists the exact environments. Llama-3.1 ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and the Tulu-3 checkpoints ( Lambert et al., 2025 ) are released under the Llama 3.1 Community License, Gemma-2 ( Gemma Team, 2024 ) under the Gemma Terms of Use, Qwen-2.5 ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , OLMo-2 ( Walsh et al., 2025 ) , and Mistral-7B ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) under Apache 2.0, and Zephyr ( Tunstall et al., 2024 ) under MIT. We use the API models ( OpenAI, 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) under their providers’ terms of service. The BCT benchmark items (MIT) are drawn from MMLU (MIT), TruthfulQA (Apache 2.0), HellaSwag, and LogiQA, and we also use SycophancyEval and the Tulu-3 SFT mixture (ODC-BY). We could not confirm a license for HellaSwag, LogiQA, or SycophancyEval. The Tulu-3 SFT subsets used for training contain prompts written by users (for example from WildChat) that we did not screen for personal or offensive content. We use all artifacts only for research evaluation and analysis, which is consistent with their intended research use, and we release only code, with no model weights or data.

sections.heading: B.2 Items, prompts, and scoring
sections.text: Each BCT item has an uncued prompt and a cued prompt that adds a cue pointing to a wrong option X X , and we keep items where X X differs from the correct option T T . Aligned models read prompts through their own chat templates, and base models in plain text receive the joined message text followed by an answer marker. The Tulu-3 chat template adds no BOS token. In the comparisons with format held fixed, both models receive identical prompts. Each graded ladder inserts one cue wording just before the answer instruction, so the strengths differ only in the cue sentence. The first ladder runs from no cue to an expert assertion, and in Tulu-3-8B it adds three prompt-injection wordings that enter only the margin relationship (Appendix H.2 ) and the rule of the strong ladder (Appendix I ). The stage tests use a weaker ladder of a passing guess by a third party, a hedge, an admission of ignorance, a random guess, and a plain opinion (“I think the answer is X”). The arithmetic items are generated problems whose answers can be computed, and presentations of the same problem differ in option order and usually in the distractor and cued values. In 24% of suggested-answer rows, and in none of the other cue types, the cued and uncued prompts are identical after the loader’s preprocessing. We exclude these items from all caving-rate and susceptibility computations, and analyses based on flips are not affected. The monitor, confidence-direction, confidence-steering, single-head ablation, and reader-rank analyses did not store per-item records, so they keep these items. Each letter’s score is the log-sum-exp of the logits at the final position over the token variants of that letter, the answer is the letter with the highest score, and probabilities are the softmax over the letters. An item is known to a model if its uncued answer is T T , and the model caves on it if its cued answer is X X . Susceptibility is Δ ​ p X \Delta p_{X} , the change in p ⁡ ( X ) p(X) from the uncued to the cued prompt. The post-cue margin is p ⁡ ( T ) − p ⁡ ( X ) p(T)-p(X) on the cued prompt, and uncued confidence is p ⁡ ( T ) − max L ≠ T ⁡ p ⁡ ( L ) p(T)-\max_{L\neq T}p(L) on the uncued prompt. Some analyses report caving as the share of all cued prompts answered with X X on a fixed item set, without restricting it to known items. These are the weight copies, fine-tuning runs, in-context and steering conditions, role control, checkpoint fingerprint, and attention dial. The fixed set is an aligned model’s flips, except that the dial, the role control, and the fixed-set check of the fine-tuning runs use unselected items, which were chosen without regard to any model’s answers.

sections.heading: B.3 Checking the letter readout
sections.text: We read answers from the letter scores. The letter set holds the bare letters and the letters with a leading space, so for the Llama-3.1/Tulu-3, OLMo-2, and Qwen-2.5 tokenizers it leaves out fused tokens such as “(B”. We checked the readout against greedy generation on 40 items per test set and checkpoint, and, for the Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B stage pairs, on 400 of the 455 published items and all 237 held-out items. For the 7B to 13B stage checkpoints and five instruct models in their chat templates, the parsed generated answer matches the readout on 94% to 100% of prompts. Including the fused tokens changes the readout on at most 5% of these prompts, and item-level susceptibility under the two readouts correlates at 0.96 or above. With the fused tokens included, the DPO-to-RL differences are almost unchanged for OLMo-2-7B and on the graded and arithmetic sets. Tulu’s differences shrink but stay significant after Bonferroni correction. On the 400 rerun published items, the difference goes from + 0.047 +0.047 to + 0.036 +0.036 ( t = 4.5 t=4.5 ), and the letter readout gives + 0.050 +0.050 on all 455 items. On the held-out cues, it goes from + 0.071 +0.071 to + 0.049 +0.049 ( t = 3.5 t=3.5 ). OLMo-2-13B’s published-cue difference, which we checked on 40 items only, goes from + 0.024 +0.024 to + 0.015 +0.015 . Base models in plain text agree less often. Agreement is 60% to 93% on the items of the format comparison (Appendix C.4 ), and 56% on 40 items for Gemma-2-2b, which often begins its answer with a newline. When we score the plain-text factorial from parsed generated answers, every change from base to aligned model keeps its direction, but OLMo-2’s increase is no longer significant ( + 0.07 +0.07 , p = 0.21 p=0.21 , Appendix C.4 ).

sections.heading: B.4 Pairing and tests
sections.text: Comparisons between base and aligned models and between stages use only items that both models answered correctly without the cue, with paired differences per item, while the layer knockout scores each model on its own known items. Caving comparisons use exact McNemar tests, and susceptibility comparisons use a paired t t test with n n equal to the number of items. On the graded, arithmetic, and 70B sets, each item’s Δ ​ p X \Delta p_{X} is averaged over the four mid-strength wordings of the ladder (hedge, admission of ignorance, random guess, and plain opinion). Presentations of the same arithmetic problem are averaged into one unit, while the chain-of-thought comparison (Appendix F.2 ) counts presentations.

sections.heading: B.5 Attention measures
sections.text: The reader attention rate is the share of items on which a designated reader’s largest attention weight falls on a token that spells the cued option’s letter. We average it over readers and measure it with eager attention at the final prompt position. The cued letter also appears outside the cue, in the list “(A, B, C, D, …)” of the answer instruction (in 92% to 95% of items) and in the option labels. Letter-based measures therefore partly track the option the model is about to choose. On the graded items with no cue at all, the Tulu and OLMo readers’ rate is 0.22 to 0.47 on items that the model answers with the cued letter, against 0.04 on items that it answers correctly. With a cue, it is 0.66 to 0.91 on caved items and 0.14 to 0.18 on resisted items. Several analyses use such measures. These are the stage-wise attention changes, the attention rates of the fine-tuning and role experiments, the attention-matching target, the checkpoint fingerprint, the item-level prediction, and the monitor. Their correlations with caving therefore overstate how much the heads read the cue. The causal claims rest on interventions that measure behavior directly. These are patching, weight copies, activation steering, the attention-pattern swap, and scaling of attention to the cue.

sections.heading: B.6 Interventions
sections.text: Activation patching replaces a head’s output at the answer position with its value from the paired uncued run. Its recovery is the fraction of cue-induced flips whose answer returns to T T . For interventions that also act on uncued prompts, preservation is the fraction of uncued prompts that keep their correct answer. Random controls are head sets of the same size drawn with fixed seeds (1 to 30 sets per condition). In the cross-family set-level patches, a new set is drawn for every flip. Attention scaling adds log ⁡ λ \log\lambda to the attention logits from each position after the cue to each cue token. It uses an additive mask in every layer and head unless a smaller set is stated. This multiplies the cue tokens’ unnormalized attention weights by λ \lambda before the softmax renormalizes each row. At λ = 0 \lambda{=}0 these links are removed, and every other link stays intact.

In the four cross-family models, a flip can also share its question with a discovery flip under another cue type. The discovery bands (layers 10 to 22 in Llama, 13 to 29 in Gemma-9B, 8 to 20 in Qwen-7B, 18 to 36 in Qwen-14B, and 13 to 18 in Gemma-2-2b) cover roughly 40 percent of each model’s depth, except the older and narrower Gemma-2-2b band, and were fixed before any ranking. The rankings for Qwen-7B and Gemma-9B also pool extension scans (layers 14 to 26 and 24 to 36, on suggested-answer flips) that we added after inspecting their main-band rankings, and the Qwen-7B readers and writers in Table 2 come from its extension scan. Table 2 summarizes the circuit in each family. Random head sets of the same size recover 0.02 to 0.05 on average for the top-8 patch and 0.03 to 0.08 for the top-16 patch, and the largest draw-series means are 0.08 and 0.11. For the Gemma-2-2b set, 30 fixed random sets reach at most 0.29 on the selection slice. What the families share is a small set of heads in middle and late layers. The head indices differ across families, and Qwen-14B is much more spread out. In plain text, the strongest of each base model’s three readers ranks first or second in attention to the cued letter among all heads of a fixed layer band, and the two strongest of the three readers rank between 1 and 7. This is a descriptive attention measure, and we did not patch single heads in base models. Qwen-14B has no designated readers, so for it we use the three heads of its instruct model that attend most to the cue. In Gemma-9B and Qwen-7B, the listed readers have near-zero recovery on their own, and so do two of the three Llama readers. Of the listed readers in these three models, only Llama’s L18.H28 is among the top-8 patched heads, so we test the flow from readers to writers only in Gemma-2-2b. Patching the early readers (L13.H6, L13.H2, L14.H2) reverses 17 of 76 suggested-answer flips. With the writers (L15.H7, L16.H4, L17.H3) frozen at their biased values, it reverses 1. A random set of three heads from the circuit band (L13 to L18) reverses 10, and 3 with the writers frozen. The writers therefore also pass on the effects of other heads in the band, so the path through the writers is not specific to the readers.

sections.heading: C.2 Leave-one-cue-out selection and single heads
sections.text: To test whether the circuit is shared causally or is a union of cue-specific parts, we rank heads using three of the four cue types and patch the top eight together on the flips of the fourth. Recovery on the held-out cue is 0.90 (suggested answer), 0.98 (prior commitment), 0.81 (distractor fact), and 0.93 (wrong few-shot) in Llama, and 0.75, 0.60, 0.69, and 0.69 in Gemma-9B, against random means of 0.01 to 0.06 (20 random draws, 32 to 40 flips per cell). Llama’s top two heads and Gemma-9B’s top three are the same in every fold. The rule that we set in advance compared each cell with the pooled top-8 recovery on that cue. We did not store that value. Every cell is within 15 points of the recovery pooled over all four cues (0.92 in Llama, 0.69 in Gemma-9B). No single head is necessary. In four of five models, mean-ablating the best of 40 to 50 searched heads lowers caving by at most 0.01 more than ablating a random head. In OLMo-2-7B the best head, L18.H19, lowers caving on items still answered correctly from 0.58 to 0.48, but it also lowers uncued accuracy from 1.00 to 0.83.

sections.heading: C.3 Weight copies and layer knockout
sections.text: The weight copies take the query and output projections of the designated heads from one model and put them into the other. These heads are three readers and three writers, which in Gemma-2-2b leaves out L13.H2, the fourth reader of the seven-head set. We then rerun the full evaluation on flip items that include the discovery slice (400 flip items of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for Tulu-3-8B-SFT, and its own flips for Gemma-2-2b-it), with random six-head sets as the control. Separate arms copy the heads’ shared key-value groups (Tulu) or one whole attention layer. Across the head and whole-layer arms, the aligned model with base weights caves at 0.81 to 0.82, compared with 0.80 without the copy (Tulu-3-SFT). For Gemma-2-2b-it the values are 0.95 to 0.99, compared with 1.00. The key-value arms give the same result. As a positive control, copying the SFT checkpoint’s weights into the Llama base changes chat-format behavior (320 flip items). The MLPs of layers 0 and 1 alone raise caving from 0.21 to 0.57 and uncued accuracy from 0.03 to 0.22, and whole layers 0 to 11 raise them to 0.90 and 0.72 (the SFT checkpoint is at 0.80 and 0.74). The layer knockout replaces one layer’s attention output at the answer position with its uncued value, for every layer in turn. The most effective layer is the same in base and aligned weights in three of five models (layer 28 in Gemma-2-9B, 17 in Llama-3.1-8B, and 36 in Qwen-2.5-14B), and it differs in Gemma-2-2b (18 against 16) and Qwen-2.5-7B (19 against 24). On average, knocking out this layer removes 51% (base) and 54% (aligned) of caving (paired t t -test over the five models, p = 0.82 p=0.82 , with wide intervals per model).

sections.heading: C.5 Beyond multiple choice
sections.text: On SycophancyEval answer sycophancy (open TriviaQA questions with a stated user belief, scored by the log-probability margin between the correct and the incorrect answer after “The answer is”), 70.6% of Gemma-2-2b’s known answers flip (154 of 218), and 25.5% of Llama-3.1-8B’s (56 of 220). Patching the circuit heads recovers 15.6% of Gemma’s flips, against 1.3 to 7.1% for five random sets of the same size. In Llama the patch reverses only 4 of 56 flips (7.1%), one more than the best random set (random sets reverse 0 to 5.4%). The circuit’s writers alone reverse 10 (17.9%). The effect also appears when the cue names no letter. When the prompt asks for the text of the option and the cue states the wrong option’s content, the patch still reverses 0.20 of flips in Gemma (random mean 0.037) and 0.15 in Llama (random mean 0.003). In Gemma, masking the six tokens that the writer hub L17.H3 attends to most restores correct free-form answers as well as masking the exact tokens of the suggested wrong answer does (0.880, compared with 0.870). A head chosen without labels to locate the cue (L16.H7) restores 0.65. Uncued accuracy on these 108 known items falls only to 0.84 (0.87 when masking a random span), while deleting the same tokens leaves 0.19.

sections.text: This section supports Section 4 .

sections.heading: D.1 Short fine-tuning runs
sections.text: The runs train rank-16 LoRA adapters ( α = 32 \alpha=32 , dropout 0, on all attention and MLP projections) on the Llama-3.1-8B base with cue-free generic or code subsets of the Tulu-3 SFT mixture. They use AdamW at learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} with no weight decay, a cosine schedule with 3% warmup, batch size 8, gradient clipping at 1.0, sequences of up to 1024 tokens, and loss on the assistant response only, for two epochs. At N = 200 N=200 this is 50 optimization steps. The comparison with the full SFT checkpoint therefore shows how little data is enough to reach SFT-level caving, and it says nothing about efficiency at matched compute. Draws differ in the training sample. Evaluation uses the chat template, on 400 flip items of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (25 per cue type and dataset), and for Gemma on Gemma-2-2b-it’s own flips. The adapters were merged into the bf16 base weights before evaluation and were not kept. Merging rounds the update to bf16, and we did not measure how much this changes the results. With 200 generic examples, the attention rate averaged over the three readers is 0.65 to 0.76 over three draws, against 0.55 for the full SFT checkpoint, and caving is 0.86 to 0.94 against 0.80. With 200 code examples (five draws), caving is 0.81 to 0.91, with a lower attention rate. Figure 2 b shows single draws at 20, 50, 1,000, and 5,000 examples and the mean and range of three draws at 200. We repeat this in Gemma-2-2b with the same data and procedure. At 200 examples, the rate of the main reader (L18.H6) goes from 0.00 to 0.79, compared with 0.90 for the tuned checkpoint. Caving reaches 0.94, compared with 1.00 for the tuned checkpoint. These items are the tuned checkpoint’s own flips. The model tuned on 200 examples answers only 0.29 of them correctly without the cue. On the unselected fixed set of the role control (Appendix D.2 ), susceptibility after 200 examples matches the tuned checkpoint in both families (0.47 in Llama and 0.45 in Gemma). To test whether the same heads carry the new caving, we patch the top eight heads of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Appendix C.1 ) in each tuned model, replacing their answer-position outputs with their uncued values. The item pool has 20 to 30 flip items of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct per cue type and dataset, including the 12 items per cell used to select these heads, and we patch on the items in this pool that the tuned model flips. The eight heads undo 0.54, 0.69, and 0.73 of the flips in the three generic models (184, 156, and 147 flips) and 0.37 to 0.58 in the five code models (75 to 169 flips). Five random sets of eight heads from layers 13 to 22 undo at most 0.03 in the generic models and 0.04 in the code models. The three designated readers alone undo at most 0.04.

sections.heading: D.4 Patching after in-context activation
sections.text: We place eight generic dialogue turns, or three multiple-choice examples, before the prompt of the Llama-3.1-8B base in the Tulu-3 chat template, on up to 40 flip items of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct per cue type and dataset, which include the 12 items per cell used to select the heads patched below. The flips caused by the context are the items that the base with this context answers correctly without the cue and with X X under it (122 with the dialogue turns and 186 with the examples). We patch the answer-position outputs of the three readers (L18.H28, L16.H19, L20.H14) and three writers (L17.H24, L15.H8, L15.H11) with their uncued values, and compare with 10 random sets of six heads from layers 13 to 20 outside these heads. The six heads undo 53% and 60% of these flips, the writers alone 48% and 54%, the readers alone 2% and 3%, and the random sets 2% and 1% on average (at most 7%).

sections.heading: E.4 Attention-pattern swap
sections.text: The swap runs identical prompts through both checkpoints and records each checkpoint’s attention patterns after the softmax. It then reruns the other checkpoint with the patterns of the chosen layers fully replaced (all heads, all positions). There is no scale parameter. A checkpoint patched with its own patterns reproduces its natural logits to four decimal places on a check prompt. On the held-out questions of the layer-set sweep ( n = 57 n=57 and 54 54 ), swapping the middle band transfers M ↓ M_{\downarrow} and M ↑ M_{\uparrow} of 0.72 0.72 and 0.73 0.73 in Tulu and 0.61 0.61 and 0.62 0.62 in OLMo, and all CIs exclude zero. Uncued answers stay correct under every swap of the middle band, the writer layer, or both (preservation 1.00), and the clean control cells keep 0.98 to 1.00. The controls ran in two waves. In the first wave, ten layer sets contain no middle-band, reader, or writer layer, and they transfer between − 0.29 -0.29 and + 0.14 +0.14 . Two Tulu random sets that contain the writer layer L17 transfer 0.63 0.63 to 0.74 0.74 , so in Tulu the first wave failed the specificity rule that we set in advance. A second wave, specified in advance, then tested the writer layer separately from the middle band, a split that we found after the first wave. In Tulu, the writer layer alone transfers 0.68 0.68 and 0.64 0.64 , and the writer layer together with the middle band transfers 0.88 0.88 and 0.89 0.89 . Twenty new random six-layer sets per pipeline, drawn without the middle-band, reader, and writer layers, transfer less than 0.3 0.3 in all eighty cells. OLMo has no separate writer layer, because its writer hub L18.H19 both reads and writes inside a reader layer. The difference is therefore largely transferred by the circuit region in the middle layers, and by none of the layer sets that we tested outside it. We found the writer-layer split on these same items, however. Swapping only the three reader layers moves behavior away from the donor in Tulu ( − 0.29 -0.29 and − 0.27 -0.27 ) and partly toward it in OLMo ( + 0.53 +0.53 and + 0.52 +0.52 ). In a first run, a generator error made six of the eight random layer sets overlap the middle band or the reader layers. We exclude all eight sets from the null result, and the released results keep them. We also swap the middle band on the two held-out cue types. The stage difference is measurable in three of the four cells of pipeline and cue, and in the fourth (OLMo, spurious few-shot) its CI spans zero. In the three measurable cells, the swap transfers M M of 0.48 0.48 to 0.78 0.78 , and every CI excludes zero. Of the 48 control cells of eight clean random six-layer sets per pipeline, 45 transfer less than 0.3 0.3 in magnitude, and the exceptions, all in Tulu, reach 0.47 0.47 (the control that failed the first run), 0.34 0.34 , and − 0.30 -0.30 . A first run with two controls per cell had specified in advance that both stay below 0.3 0.3 , and one Tulu control reached 0.47 0.47 . The criterion for eight controls (at least 90% of control cells below 0.3 0.3 ) was set after that run and before the run with eight controls.

sections.heading: E.5 Query, key, and value states
sections.text: Swapping the donor’s query and key states together reproduces the pattern swap exactly, as a consistency check. The query side alone carries most of the difference in OLMo ( 0.57 0.57 and 0.54 0.54 ) and the largest single share in Tulu ( 0.50 0.50 and 0.46 0.46 ), and the key side carries less ( 0.45 0.45 and 0.35 0.35 in Tulu, 0.22 0.22 and 0.24 0.24 in OLMo). Donor values under the receiving model’s own patterns carry part of the difference in Tulu ( 0.38 0.38 and 0.33 0.33 ) and less than 0.3 in OLMo ( 0.21 0.21 and 0.28 0.28 ), below the partial band. Every CI excludes zero. These are tests of causal sufficiency, so the shares need not add up. The expectation set in advance that donor values fall in the null band (below 0.3) is not met in Tulu. We also test a single fixed query shift per middle-band layer. The shift is the mean difference between DPO and RL in the final-position query on the calibration half. It reproduces the query-side swap in Tulu ( 0.51 0.51 and 0.50 0.50 ). In OLMo it reproduces only 40% to 44% of the query-side swap ( 0.23 0.23 and 0.24 0.24 ), which misses the threshold of 0.3 0.3 that we set in advance. Random shifts of the same norm transfer − 0.05 -0.05 to 0.00 0.00 .

sections.heading: E.6 The middle band in the pretrained base
sections.text: In the pretrained base models in plain text, we scale the middle band’s attention to the cue over λ ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 1 , 2 , 4 } \lambda\in\{0,0.25,0.5,1,2,4\} . We measure susceptibility on the items that each base answers correctly without the cue (51 in Tulu, 50 in OLMo). In the Tulu base (Llama-3.1-8B) it is 0.05, 0.11, 0.14, 0.18, 0.21, and 0.23, rising at every step. In the OLMo base it is 0.02, 0.16, 0.25, 0.32, 0.34, and 0.32, dipping at 4. The rule that we set in advance required a middle-band response that rises at every step and is larger than the responses of the low and high bands. This rule holds in Tulu but not in OLMo. The high band is flat in OLMo and moves Tulu only slightly (0.17 to 0.20), and the low band is flat in Tulu while moving in the opposite direction in OLMo (0.35 down to 0.22). Scaling at the reader heads barely moves susceptibility in Tulu (0.19 to 0.17). In OLMo it also moves susceptibility (0.23 to 0.37), which fits the partial transfer through OLMo’s reader heads (Appendix E.3 ).

sections.heading: E.7 Reader attention across stages
sections.text: On a subset of the graded items ( n = 121 n=121 Tulu, 114 114 OLMo), the readers’ attention rate to the cued letter rises from DPO to the RL stage (Tulu + 0.052 +0.052 , t = 5.5 t=5.5 , and OLMo + 0.064 +0.064 , t = 6.5 t=6.5 ). On the published four-cue items, the rate rises in OLMo ( t = 2.5 t=2.5 ). In Tulu the rise is not significant ( t = 1.1 t=1.1 ), which misses the criterion that we set in advance (a positive change with | t | > 2 |t|>2 ). Tulu’s prior-commitment cell falls ( − 0.058 -0.058 , t = − 3.3 t=-3.3 ), while the susceptibility for that cue does not. We also measure the attention margin, the readers’ attention mass on the cued option’s letter minus their mass on the correct option’s letter. It rises in both pipelines ( t = 16.1 t=16.1 in Tulu and 13.6 13.6 in OLMo, on 150 and 139 items). The readers’ total attention mass on the cue text rises in Tulu ( + 0.024 +0.024 , t = 15.3 t=15.3 ) and falls in OLMo ( − 0.009 -0.009 , t = − 5.3 t=-5.3 ). In OLMo, however, the letter-based rate and caving both rise ( + 0.064 +0.064 and + 0.057 +0.057 ). The letter-based measures partly track the chosen answer (Appendix B.5 ), so this mismatch may partly reflect attention to the chosen answer.

sections.heading: F.2 Reasoning before answering
sections.text: We use identical cue wording (“I think the answer is X.”) and items answered correctly in both answering modes. On arithmetic, reasoning before answering cuts Tulu’s caving from 0.79 to 0.19 at DPO and from 0.90 to 0.01 at RLVR. On knowledge questions it cuts caving only from 0.88 to 0.63 and from 0.96 to 0.65 (Figure 8 pools the stages). Pooled over stages, the interaction is + 0.46 +0.46 (unpaired z = + 7.0 z=+7.0 ). Its unit is one presentation of an item at a stage, with 111 knowledge and 129 arithmetic presentations. Counting each distinct arithmetic prompt once per stage gives + 0.55 +0.55 ( z = + 7.4 z=+7.4 ). An automatic parser reads the final answers and misreads some chains that are cut off or that correct themselves, and we report the parsed values. This pattern is consistent with the idea that deriving an answer restores the margin more than reasoning about a knowledge question does, and it separates two kinds of question that Feng et al. (2026) pool as objective tasks. A keyword search flags 2 of the 109 caved knowledge chains in the Tulu-3 and OLMo-2 checkpoints, and when we read these two, neither refers to the cue. Nine of the stored traces are cut off at 1,200 characters. Reasoning models state such hints more often than non-reasoning models, though still in a minority of cases ( Chen et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: G.2 Two-turn span masking
sections.text: The scripted assistant reply after the user’s challenge is a fixed turn that names another option in about 40% of items. On items that the model answers correctly before the challenge, we set to zero the attention to both the challenge and this reply. This removes retraction (0 of 220 items in Llama-3.1-8B and 2 of 402 in Gemma-2-2b, against natural rates of 0.33 and 0.36), while masking the challenge alone leaves 0.30 and 0.27, and masking the reply alone leaves 0.36 and 0.18. With both spans masked, the effective context reduces to the question, the scripted correct first answer, and the final request, so the complete removal partly reflects this reduced context. Masking only in the six-layer band chosen in advance (layers 10 to 15 of 32 in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and 13 to 18 of 26 in Gemma-2-2b-it) removes retraction as completely as masking every layer (Llama 0.37 to 0.00, n = 451 n=451 , and Gemma 0.36 to 0.01, n = 402 n=402 ), while random six-layer bands outside the circuit layers leave it at 0.36. sections.text: In five models, attention to every occurrence of the cued letter separates caving from resisting items on held-out questions. Held-out AUROC is 0.91 to 0.995 on the cue types used for selection, and 0.985 and 0.998 on two held-out cue types in Gemma-2-2b (Figure 10 ). sections.heading: J.1 Mechanistic studies of post-training
sections.text: Related studies compare RL and SFT features trained from one base on identical data ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , and find instruction representations acting as circuit selectors across OLMo-2 base, SFT, and DPO checkpoints ( Bigoulaeva et al., 2026 ) . Others report higher activation intensity and less concentrated edge activations after online RL (PPO, GRPO), with weaker or inconsistent changes after DPO ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Further studies report that gains in context grounding from SFT and DPO largely reuse machinery present in the starting model ( Gupta and Gupta, 2026 ) , that fine-tuning strengthens an existing entity-tracking circuit ( Prakash et al., 2024 ) , that it can act as a thin wrapper around existing abilities ( Jain et al., 2024 ) , and that DPO routes around a pretrained ability and leaves it in place ( Lee et al., 2024 ) . Others follow how circuits change across fine-tuning checkpoints ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) .

sections.heading: J.2 Locating sycophancy and cue-following
sections.text: Sycophancy has been located in heads found by path patching and then fine-tuned ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , in head activations that can be decoded linearly ( Genadi et al., 2026 ) , and in steering directions that separate sycophantic behaviors ( Vennemeyer et al., 2026 ) . It has also been located in error-detection heads present in a base model and kept across later aligned releases ( Pandey, 2026 ) , in modes that are distinct in representation but share most of their attention heads ( Jain et al., 2026 ) , and in late layers where user opinions override factual knowledge ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Each of these studies uses released checkpoints or pairs of models before and after a single alignment or fine-tuning step. None follows the successive stages of one post-training pipeline. Kumarappan and Mujoo (2026) find that base models yield to simulated peer pressure as much as or more than their instruct versions in 10 of 12 cells of family and condition, and they locate the effect in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct in attention in layers 14 to 18. Tracing persona directions finds sycophancy directions forming early in pretraining and, across the SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of OLMo-3, persona suppression concentrated at the DPO stage ( Moskvoretskii et al., 2026 ) . Related heads copy wrong labels from demonstrations ( Halawi et al., 2024 ) and select multiple-choice answer letters ( Lieberum et al., 2023 ; Wiegreffe et al., 2025 ) , and the heads we study may overlap with such answer-selection heads. Different biases can also occupy different directions in the hidden states ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) . Our comparison with the format held fixed suggests one reason why chat-format comparisons of base and final models, including direction-level work that attributes susceptibility to alignment tuning ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) , can seem to show that alignment builds the circuit. Consistency training partly transfers to held-out biases ( Chua et al., 2025 ; Imran et al., 2026 ) and, in one model, from jailbreaks to sycophancy ( Gautam et al., 2026 ) , which a shared circuit could explain.

sections.heading: J.3 Interventions on attention
sections.text: Rescaling attention weights or head outputs can shift models between facts in the prompt and facts in memory ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Ortu et al., 2024 ) , and attention steering can help them follow highlighted text ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Concurrent work uses attention steering to reduce sycophancy ( He et al., 2026 ) . Suppressing unsupported agreement tends to harm updating on real evidence ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and resisting wrong suggestions and accepting correct ones are distinct abilities ( Sinha, 2026 ) . He et al. (2026) report that suppressing attention to user pressure while also amplifying attention to supplied context lowers pressure following and improves updating on that context, although their method suppresses a user’s stated answer whether or not it is correct. We measure this trade-off for scaling attention to the cue (§ 7 ).

text: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved.
